The evidence from multiple high-credibility sources consistently supports the conclusion that strict gun control laws are associated with decreased gun violence. A peer-reviewed study published in Pediatrics found "an important association between firearm legislation and pediatric firearm-related mortality," noting that "states with more firearm laws had lower rates of firearm fatalities in a population of adults and children" [d5]. A BMJ time trends analysis found that "US states with more relaxed gun control laws and higher rates of gun ownership have higher rates of mass shootings," with the gap between permissive and restrictive states widening in recent years [d2]. The APA reports that "firearm prohibitions for high-risk groups…have been shown to reduce violence," and that licensing, background checks, and oversight of gun sellers "can reduce the diversion of guns to criminals" [d3]. The AAFP similarly notes that "background checks for ammunition purchases, limits on ammunition purchases, and identification requirements for firearms, have been shown to reduce firearm deaths," and that CAP laws "decrease firearm-related self-injuries…among all ages, and decrease unintentional firearm injuries and death among children" [d1]. While some opponents argue that gun control does not effectively regulate firearm-related deaths, the statistical evidence cited across sources suggests that "when access to guns is controlled, the rate of homicides is likely to go down" [d4].
